The chapter's analysis of the tangent at a point on the circle states the property it rests on: 'a line perpendicular to the radius at its outer end is a tangent to the circle. If CP is a radius with point P on the circle, line \(l\) through P and perpendicular to CP is the tangent at P.'

Through a given point on a given line there is exactly one perpendicular to that line. \(\therefore\) at a point on the circle exactly one tangent can be drawn.

The number of tangents is 1.

\(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR\), so the corresponding sides are proportional:

\(\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{BC}{QR} = \dfrac{AC}{PR} = \dfrac{7}{5}\)

\(\dfrac{7}{5} > 1\), so \(AB > PQ\), and the same holds for each of the other two pairs of corresponding sides.

\(\therefore\) every side of \(\triangle ABC\) is longer than the corresponding side of \(\triangle PQR\), so \(\triangle ABC\) is bigger.

The chapter uses exactly this reasoning in Ex. (2): from \(\dfrac{AB}{A'B} = \dfrac{5}{3}\) it concludes 'sides of \(\triangle ABC\) are longer than corresponding sides of \(\triangle A'BC'\)'.
